title: Is Industrial Maintenance a Good Career?
description: See what industrial maintenance technicians do, how training works, what the job pays, and whether the schedule fits your goals.
author: Career Education Institute Curriculum Team
coverAlt: Industrial maintenance technician inspecting a conveyor motor with safety gear in a factory
body:
Is industrial maintenance a good career? It can be a strong choice if you like figuring out why machines fail, working with your hands, and learning mechanical and electrical systems. Industrial maintenance technicians keep factory equipment running by inspecting, troubleshooting and repairing conveyors, motors, pumps, hydraulics, pneumatics and automated controls. The field also offers a clear training path and projected growth, but rotating shifts, call-ins and machinery hazards are real parts of the work.

## What does an industrial maintenance technician do?

Industrial maintenance technicians protect production time and worker safety. When a line stops, they gather information, isolate the problem and restore the equipment according to the site’s procedures. They may investigate a failed bearing, misaligned shaft, hydraulic leak, tripped motor or faulty sensor in a programmable logic controller, also called a PLC.

The job is not only emergency repair. A technician also performs preventive maintenance on a schedule and predictive maintenance by watching signs such as vibration and temperature. The goal is to find wear before it becomes a breakdown. Technicians document work orders and repairs in a computerized maintenance management system, or CMMS, so the team can see equipment history and plan future work.

Common responsibilities include:

- Inspecting belts, bearings, motors, pumps and other equipment
- Troubleshooting mechanical, electrical, hydraulic and pneumatic problems
- Reading schematics, prints and PLC ladder logic
- Aligning shafts and adjusting machinery
- Locking out and tagging out equipment before service
- Recording findings, repairs and parts in the CMMS

You can see the full duties, tools and work settings in the [industrial maintenance technician career profile](/careers/industrial-maintenance-technician/).

## Is industrial maintenance a good career for your work style?

This career fits people who enjoy practical problem-solving and can stay methodical under pressure. You may need to move from a symptom to a root cause instead of replacing the first part that looks suspicious. You also need to communicate with operators, supervisors and other technicians while a production line is waiting.

The work is usually indoors, but a plant can be noisy, hot or fast-paced. You may work around moving machinery and stored energy, so safety procedures are part of the job rather than an optional extra. Lockout and tagout procedures control hazardous energy, and technicians must verify zero energy before beginning maintenance.

Ask yourself:

- Do I like understanding how machines work?
- Can I combine mechanical, electrical and computer-based troubleshooting?
- Am I willing to follow detailed safety procedures every time?
- Can I stay calm when equipment is down and people need answers?
- Am I comfortable with rotating shifts, overtime or call-ins?

> Tip: A realistic job preview should include the schedule and safety environment, not only the pay. Ask an employer what a normal shift, call-in rotation and training period look like.

## What is the schedule like?

Industrial maintenance is often full-time. Plants that run around the clock may use rotating shifts, and overtime or call-ins can happen when equipment breaks down. A maintenance department may start with a shift handoff, review downtime reports, complete scheduled inspections, respond to a stopped conveyor and close work orders before the shift ends.

That variety can be appealing if you prefer active work over a desk routine. It can be difficult if you need a predictable Monday-through-Friday schedule. Before accepting a role, ask whether the position is on first, second or third shift, how often schedules rotate, and how the employer handles breakdowns outside normal hours.

## How do you train for industrial maintenance?

The site lists a high school diploma as typically required. Many technicians complete a one- to two-year technical program in industrial maintenance or mechatronics, enter an apprenticeship, or build skills through extensive on-the-job training. The career profile lists a broader training range of one to four years because employers and roles differ.

Training usually builds from basic maintenance to more complex systems. You may start by learning tools, measurements, preventive maintenance and safe work practices. As you gain experience, you can add motor controls, electrical troubleshooting, hydraulics, pneumatics, PLC basics, ladder logic, vibration analysis and shaft alignment.

A practical preparation plan looks like this:

1. Finish high school or confirm that your diploma or equivalent meets the employer’s requirement.
2. Strengthen math, measurement and technical reading skills.
3. Compare industrial maintenance, mechatronics and electromechanical programs.
4. Look for helper, technician I or apprenticeship openings where you can learn under supervision.
5. Build electrical and PLC skills after you understand basic mechanical maintenance.

The [industrial maintenance training page](/training/industrial-maintenance-technician/) can help you compare a course-based starting point with the broader path described in the [how to become an industrial maintenance technician guide](/careers/industrial-maintenance-technician/how-to-become/). Training can prepare you for entry-level work, but it does not guarantee a job or a particular outcome.

## What skills matter most?

Industrial maintenance is a multi-skill career. Mechanical knowledge helps you understand bearings, belts, gearboxes and alignment. Electrical and controls knowledge helps you trace power, interpret sensors and understand how a PLC controls a machine. Hydraulics and pneumatics add another layer of systems to diagnose.

Employers also need technicians who document carefully and communicate clearly. A repair that is not recorded can be repeated by the next shift. A clear handoff can prevent a small issue from becoming another unplanned stop.

The most useful skills to build include:

- Mechanical troubleshooting and preventive maintenance
- Electrical and motor controls
- PLC basics and ladder logic
- Hydraulics and pneumatics
- Bearing care and shaft alignment
- Problem-solving under pressure
- Teamwork, communication and documentation

Credentials may include CMRT, NIMS credentials, OSHA 10 General Industry or NFPA 70E training, depending on the role and employer. Treat each credential as a possible skill signal, not a universal requirement. Read the job posting and ask which training the employer provides.

## What is the pay and job outlook?

The labor data used on this site covers industrial machinery mechanics, the BLS occupation connected to industrial maintenance technicians. The median wage is $64,520, with the 10th percentile at $46,120, the 25th percentile at $55,010, the 75th percentile at $78,780 and the 90th percentile at $95,170. These figures are BLS, May 2025. They describe the occupation across the United States, not a guaranteed starting wage or a specific offer.

Employment is projected to grow 17.8% from 2025 to 2035, with about 44,400 annual openings. The data lists employment of 446,900. Your actual opportunity can vary by location, plant, experience, shift, specialty and employer. Overtime and shift premiums may affect an individual paycheck, but they should not be treated as guaranteed.

Use the [industrial maintenance salary page](/careers/industrial-maintenance-technician/salary/) to keep the wage figures connected to the occupation’s duties and requirements. A strong outlook is useful, but fit still matters. A job that pays well on paper may not suit you if the shift, environment or safety expectations conflict with your priorities.

## What are the advantages and tradeoffs?

Industrial maintenance can offer hands-on variety, a path into automation or reliability work, and a way to keep building skills after you enter the field. The work connects directly to production, so you can often see the result of a good repair or a better preventive-maintenance plan.

The tradeoffs deserve equal attention:

- Shift work and call-ins can affect sleep and family routines.
- Production pressure can make breakdowns stressful.
- Moving machinery and stored energy require disciplined safety practices.
- The learning curve is long because equipment combines many systems.
- Some facilities are noisy, hot or physically demanding.

Possible next roles include Maintenance Technician II or III, controls technician, reliability technician, maintenance supervisor or reliability engineer. Advancement is not automatic, but the skills you build can support several directions within maintenance and manufacturing.

## How can you decide before enrolling?

Start with evidence about your own fit. Read the career profile, compare the schedule with your responsibilities, and look at entry-level job postings in the area where you want to work. Note which skills employers repeat and which shifts they advertise.

Then make a short comparison table for two or three training options. Check the length, hands-on practice, equipment covered, class schedule, cost and support for finding work. Ask whether the program includes mechanical systems, electrical controls, PLCs, hydraulics, pneumatics and safety.

You can also speak with a current technician or maintenance supervisor. Ask what surprised them about the job, which skills they use most often, and what they wish they had learned first. Their experience can add context to the wage and outlook data without replacing your own research.

## Next steps

Industrial maintenance can be a good career if you want hands-on troubleshooting, can learn across mechanical and electrical systems, and accept the possibility of rotating shifts. The occupation has a projected 17.8% growth rate from 2025 to 2035, but the daily schedule and safety environment should be part of your decision.

Review the [industrial maintenance technician profile](/careers/industrial-maintenance-technician/), compare the [training option](/training/industrial-maintenance-technician/), and check the [Career Match Quiz](/quizzes/career-match/) if you are comparing technical careers. If you are ready to explore programs, use the [apprenticeships guide](/guides/apprenticeships-guide/) to prepare better questions for schools and employers.
